one_liner: Pure-JavaScript DEFLATE/gzip/zlib/ZIP codec, up to 25% faster decode and 50% faster encode than pako.
what_it_does: Compresses and decompresses raw DEFLATE, gzip, zlib and ZIP in plain JavaScript/TypeScript for browsers, Node, Deno and Bun, with no native code. The API is its own: one-shot functions on Uint8Array (deflateSync, gunzipSync, zipSync, unzipSync, decompressSync with format autodetection), push-style streaming classes (Deflate, Gunzip, Zip, Unzip), and async variants that run the same code in a Web Worker or Node worker_thread. Output is standard DEFLATE, so any zlib can read it and vice versa.
how_it_is_fast: Derived from UZIP.js rather than a line-by-line zlib port: the inflater decodes through flat 2^maxbits lookup tables (one typed-array read per symbol, 16-bit bit-reader), and the deflater uses a hash-chain LZ77 matcher with a 'nice length' early exit and a trick that re-hashes on the rarest 2-byte sequence inside the current match to cut chain walks. Everything works on typed arrays with closures avoided in hot loops (the source notes 'closures have awful performance'), and gzip/ZIP decompression preallocates the output from the stored size so the buffer is never grown. The async API parallelises multi-file ZIP across workers.
when_to_use: Browser or edge-runtime code that needs synchronous, in-memory gzip/zlib/DEFLATE (CompressionStream is stream-only and has no level control).
Replacing pako in a JS bundle: decompression-only build is about 3 kB minified versus 45.6 kB for pako.
Creating or reading ZIP archives client-side, with per-file levels and a filter to skip entries before inflating.
Multi-file ZIP compression of large files where the async API can use several worker threads.
A C++ host that already embeds a JS engine (V8, QuickJS) and must keep compression inside script code.
when_not_to_use: Any native C or C++ program: by the README's own figures fflate is about 30% slower than native zlib in decompression and 10% slower in compression, and the catalogue's zlib-ng, libdeflate and ISA-L are much faster than zlib itself.
Node services that can use the built-in zlib bindings; the author recommends those for best performance.
Untrusted input where integrity matters: the sync decoders do not verify the gzip CRC-32, the zlib Adler-32 or ZIP entry CRCs (read in src/index.ts), so corruption is not detected.

Streaming Deflate/Zip/ZipDeflate at levels 2-9 on v0.8.x: open issues #260 and #282 (May and June 2026) report output with invalid back-references that zlib rejects; zipSync and deflateSync are not affected per the reporters.
Small payloads (under about 50 kB) through the async API: worker start-up costs about 50 ms per function.

integration.min_toolchain: Any ES3-level JavaScript engine with typed arrays (README); async API needs Worker or Node worker_threads; TypeScript typings shipped
integration.platforms: any JavaScript runtime (browsers back to IE11 for workers, Node, Deno, Bun); not callable from C++ without an embedded JS engine
integration.thread_safety: Sync functions are pure over their inputs; stream objects are single-owner; async APIs run on separate workers.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: produces and reads the same formats as pako/zlib, but the API differs from pako's (different function names, Uint8Array only, callbacks for async)

gotchas: gunzipSync allocates the output from the 4-byte ISIZE trailer and unzipSync from the ZIP header size, and a caller-supplied buffer is never grown; from the source, a wrong or wrapped (over 4 GiB) size leads to silently truncated output since typed-array writes past the end are dropped and no checksum is checked.

Issue #298 (Sept 2026, open): unzipSync treats ZIP64 0xFFFFFFFF size sentinels as real sizes when there is no ZIP64 end-of-central-directory locator and tries a ~4 GiB allocation on a 33 MiB file; the streaming Unzip handles it. A tiny crafted archive can trigger large allocations the same way.
The sync API has no output-size cap, so decompression bombs must be limited by the caller (unzip filter on originalSize helps only for ZIP).
Async APIs serialise functions into workers by name-recovery tricks; issues #288 (minified builds), #266 (Deno) and #294 (Firefox WebExtensions) report breakage in some bundlers and sandboxes.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Only when the code must stay in JavaScript: every C/C++ sibling (zlib-ng, libdeflate, miniz, Wuffs) beats it and native zlib on raw speed, and Zippy plays the same role for Nim. Pick fflate over pako-style JS ports, not over native libraries.
verified_claims_summary: First-party README table rates fflate against pako as up to 25% faster in decompression and up to 50% faster in compression, with no data, runtime version, CPU or flags published; npm test writes timings to test/results but none are checked in. The same README states it is about 30% slower than native zlib to decompress and 10% slower to compress.
status_note: Active (v0.8.3, last commit May 2026) and MIT-licensed (0BSD for SheetJS), with about 3.0k stars, but several data-corruption reports against the streaming compressor from 2026 are still open with no maintainer reply visible.
